summary: A snapshot of which protocols were official Internet standards, along with Best Current Practice RFCs, as of October 25, 2001. It is a list, not a full index of the RFC series, and the current version was designated STD 1. This snapshot is historic and was replaced by RFC 3300.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a school report card for Internet rules, showing which ones had earned official status on one particular day in 2001. Later report cards replaced it.

questions: what protocols are official internet standards
subtitle: A snapshot of Internet protocol standards as of October 2001.

tldr.problem: Internet developers and administrators need to know which protocols have reached official standardization status and at what level.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3000 provides a periodic snapshot of all standardized Internet protocols, organized by standardization stage (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Historic) and also lists Best Current Practice documents.
tldr.outcome: This document serves as STD 1, the official list, but is now historic. It was replaced by RFC 3300, which provides a more current snapshot.

facts.label: Protocol categories
facts.value: 6 (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Historic, BCP)

today: RFC 3000 is Historic and has been superseded by RFC 3300, which provides a more current snapshot of Internet protocol standards. It remains a useful historical document showing the state of Internet standardization in 2001.

sections.title: Overview of Internet Standards
sections.content:
RFC 3000 contains a snapshot of the standardization status of protocols used in the Internet as of October 25, 2001. It is designated STD 1 and lists official protocol standards, Best Current Practice (BCP) documents, and other protocols at various stages of development. The RFC is not a complete index to all RFC documents, but rather focuses on those that represent actual protocol standards.

The document is published by the RFC Editor for the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), the Internet Architecture Board (IAB), and the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG). It follows the procedures specified in RFC 2026, the Internet Standards Process.
sections.plainLanguage: This document lists all the Internet rules that had been officially approved or were being worked on as of one specific date in 2001. It shows how mature each rule was.

sections.title: Standardization Levels
sections.content:
Protocols in RFC 3000 are organized into several categories based on their standardization level. Standard (or Internet Standard) protocols have gone through the full IETF process and are ready for widespread use. Draft Standard protocols are nearly complete but not yet fully approved. Proposed Standard protocols have been submitted but may still change. Experimental protocols are being tried out and may not be suitable for production use. Historic protocols are no longer recommended for use, often because they have been superseded by newer specifications.

The document also lists Best Current Practice (BCP) documents, which provide guidance on how to implement standards but are not protocol specifications themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols are grouped by how ready they are to use: some are fully approved and safe to use everywhere, some are still being tested, some are old and no longer recommended, and some are helpful guidelines rather than rules.

sections.title: Accessing Protocol Information
sections.content:
The RFC provides multiple ways to access standardization information. The most current version of the official standards list is always available on the RFC Editor web site, updated daily. Users can retrieve documents via FTP from ftp.rfc-editor.org, browse the RFC Editor's web pages at rfc-editor.org, or use email-based retrieval services.

The document lists several hundred protocols across all standardization levels, organized both by STD number (for standards) and by RFC number, making it easy to look up where a particular protocol stands in the standards process.
sections.plainLanguage: The document tells you where to find each Internet rule, both on the web and through email, so you can look up any rule you're curious about.

sections.title: Key Protocols in the Standards
sections.content:
RFC 3000 lists many foundational Internet protocols that reached Standard status, including the Internet Protocol (IP) from RFC 791, the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) from RFC 793, the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) from RFC 768, the Domain Name System (DNS) from RFCs 1034 and 1035, and the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) from RFC 821.

The Draft Standard and Proposed Standard sections show work in progress on emerging technologies of the time, such as IPv6 and various management protocols. Historic protocols like the old Routing Information Protocol are marked as replaced by newer versions.
sections.plainLanguage: The list includes famous protocols like IP and TCP that make the Internet work, plus many others for sending mail, translating names to addresses, and managing networks.

sections.title: The Standards Process
sections.content:
All protocols listed in RFC 3000 have been subject to the Internet Standards Process defined in RFC 2026. This process requires proposals to go through stages of increasing review and acceptance before reaching Standard status. The process includes technical review, implementation experience, and community consensus.

Protocols move between stages as they mature or, in some cases, are replaced by better solutions. The asterisks in RFC 3000's tables mark changes from the previous edition, helping readers see what has moved to a new status or is newly standardized.
sections.plainLanguage: To become an official Internet rule, a proposal must go through a careful review process where many experts check it and try using it. The document shows which rules recently changed their status.
